analysis.one_liner: Lets maritime workers' families sue vessel owners for full damages, including punitive damages, instead of the capped amounts allowed by an 1851 law.
analysis.headline: Introduced a month after the BP Deepwater Horizon disaster killed 11 workers, the bill to strip shipowners' liability caps died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rolled back a set of 19th-century maritime laws that shield shipowners. It repealed the Limitation of Liability Act of 1851, which lets a shipowner cap its total liability at the value of the ship and its cargo; allowed punitive damages in maritime injury cases; let families of workers killed at sea recover for loss of companionship and the victim's pain and suffering, which current law excludes; and let foreign workers injured or killed on offshore energy projects in other countries' waters sue in U.S. maritime courts. The effective date covered claims arising after April 19, 2010 — the day before the Deepwater Horizon rig exploded — and cases still in court, tying the bill directly to the BP spill litigation.
analysis.who_benefits: Seamen, offshore energy workers, and the families of maritime workers killed on the job — including non-citizen workers — would gain the right to full compensation: no cap on a shipowner's total liability, punitive damages for reckless conduct, and recovery for loss of companionship and the victim's pain and suffering. Coastal communities and taxpayers would also gain indirectly, because companies that cause catastrophes could no longer cap their payouts below the real damage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Maritime and offshore workers and their families

how_it_helps.text: It repealed the Limitation of Liability Act of 1851, which lets a shipowner cap its total liability at the value of the vessel and freight — a limit that becomes trivially small against a modern catastrophe and can leave injured workers and communities undercompensated.
It allowed punitive damages in maritime cases without regard to the amount of compensatory damages, giving juries a tool to punish reckless conduct.

It amended the Death on the High Seas Act so families could recover for nonpecuniary losses — loss of care, comfort, and companionship — plus the decedent's pain and suffering, which current law excludes, limiting recovery to purely financial losses.
It amended the Jones Act so a seaman's family could recover for loss of care, comfort, and companionship after a work-related death.

It removed restrictions barring workers who are not U.S. citizens or permanent residents from suing a mineral or energy company under U.S. maritime law for injury or death in a foreign country's territorial waters or continental shelf.

analysis.who_pays: Vessel owners, offshore drillers, and their insurers would bear uncapped liability, punitive damages, and broader wrongful-death awards. Some of that cost would pass through to shipping customers and consumers in higher prices, which supporters viewed as the true price of maritime risk rather than a subsidy from the public.
analysis.who_pays_short: Vessel owners, offshore drillers, and insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill applied retroactively: it covered not only new claims but also pending cases not yet finally decided, changing the legal rules mid-litigation for companies and insurers that had priced contracts and coverage under the old caps.

Repealing the 1851 liability cap outright removed any limit on a shipowner's exposure, which shipowners and their insurers argued could raise insurance and shipping costs and complicate financing of vessels; those costs would partly reach consumers.

Allowing foreign workers to sue energy companies under U.S. maritime law for injuries in other countries' waters would have extended U.S. courts into foreign territory, raising international-friction objections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people the bill covered — offshore and maritime workers and their families — the gains were substantial: uncapped liability, punitive damages, and compensation for non-economic losses after a death. The main costs fall on vessel owners, offshore drillers, and their insurers, and would likely trickle into shipping and energy prices. The bill's weakest points are retroactive application to cases already in court and the removal of the 1851 liability cap without a replacement limit, which its opponents would argue creates unpredictable exposure; supporters would reply that a cap set in 1851 is a poor fit for modern catastrophes. On balance it shifts risk from workers and the public to the companies that profit from maritime work.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rockefeller introduced the bill on July 15, 2010, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote appears in the action history for the remainder of the 111th Congress.

The bill took effect for causes of action arising after April 19, 2010 — the day before the Deepwater Horizon drilling rig exploded — and also reached cases then pending that had not been finally decided.
Only two of the Senate's 56 Democrats cosponsored the bill, and no Republican signed on.

The CRS summary shows the bill's substance: repealing the 1851 shipowner liability cap, authorizing punitive damages, expanding wrongful-death recovery under the Death on the High Seas Act and the Jones Act, and opening U.S. courts to foreign workers injured offshore.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Vessel owners, offshore drillers, and their insurers keep the 1851 liability cap and the limits on wrongful-death damages, and face no retroactive exposure from pending spill litigation. Workers' families remain limited to the older, narrower remedies.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Vessel owners, offshore drillers, and insurers

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 15, 2010, three months after the Deepwater Horizon disaster.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no Republican cosponsors and only 2 of 56 Senate Democrats signed on, so it never built the coalition needed to move even within its own party.

industries.industry: Offshore oil and gas drillers and contractors
industries.note: Drillers could no longer cap their total liability under the 1851 Act, would face punitive damages, and could be sued by their foreign-national workers for offshore injuries. Their financial interest ran against the workers and coastal communities exposed to their operations.

industries.industry: Shipping companies, vessel owners, and maritime insurers
industries.note: Vessel owners would lose the statutory liability cap and face broader wrongful-death damages, raising their exposure and insurance costs. That cost shift is the price of full compensation for maritime workers and their families.
